title: UP Judge Behind Gyanvapi Survey Hands Down 13 Death Sentences in Three Months
excerpt: Judge Ravi Kumar Diwakar, posted in Muzaffarnagar, sentenced 13 convicts to death across six murder trials between April and July 2026, reigniting debate over capital punishment at the district level.
body:
• Judge Ravi Kumar Diwakar sentenced 13 convicts to death across six murder trials in Muzaffarnagar between April and July 2026
  • Diwakar previously gained national attention for ordering the video survey of the Gyanvapi mosque complex in Varanasi in 2022
  • Cases ranged from a 2019 abduction-murder over a financial dispute to a 15-year-old double murder of a woman and her six-year-old son
  • All 13 sentences require confirmation by the Allahabad High Court before they can be carried out

A Record Pace of Capital Sentences

A judicial officer in Uttar Pradesh has drawn renewed scrutiny for handing down 13 death sentences across six distinct murder trials in exactly three months — an extraordinary rate that has divided legal opinion on the application of capital punishment at the district level.

https://x.com/ndtv/status/2089276273407533542

Judge Ravi Kumar Diwakar, an Additional District and Sessions Judge in Muzaffarnagar, pronounced the sentences between April 6 and July 6, 2026, according to Lawbeat. Diwakar had previously made national headlines in May 2022 for ordering the initial video survey of the Gyanvapi mosque complex in Varanasi, adjacent to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple — an order the Supreme Court later set aside and transferred to a more senior judicial officer.

The Cases

The sheer volume of capital punishments stems from a backlog of gruesome, often decades-old murder trials now reaching their conclusion.

On April 6, Diwakar sentenced three men to death for the 2019 abduction and murder of Advocate Sameer Saifi over a ₹40 lakh financial dispute. In the same month, he awarded death to a 60-year-old man and his three sons for beating a man named Shekhar to death with bricks over a ₹70,000 loan — a rare ruling against an entire family.

On May 30, a man named Rahis was sentenced to death for a 15-year-old case in which he killed a 30-year-old woman and her six-year-old son by bludgeoning them with bricks in a sugarcane field. In June, two more convicts received death sentences for a separate murder, followed by a case in which a man was sentenced for fatally stabbing a home guard who intervened to stop him from assaulting his mother.

"Democracy is based on the ballot, not the bullet."

— Judge Ravi Kumar Diwakar, while sentencing a former village head for election-related murder

The 13th death sentence came on July 6, when a former village head and his aide were convicted for the 2010 murder of a farmer over a panchayat election rivalry.

Praise and Controversy

Government advocates in Muzaffarnagar have praised the verdicts, arguing that decisive rulings on long-pending cases restore public faith in the justice system. Diwakar found that all cases met the Supreme Court's 'rarest of rare' threshold for imposing the death penalty.

But Diwakar's tenure has drawn criticism on other fronts. The Allahabad High Court previously expunged remarks in which he praised Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath in a judicial order, calling them "unwarranted expressions containing political overtones," according to Bar and Bench. In a separate order, the judge made controversial comments characterizing interfaith marriages as part of a "love jihad" conspiracy.

Diwakar has also faced persistent security threats linked to his 2022 Gyanvapi order. An NIA court judge wrote to the Allahabad High Court seeking enhanced protection for Diwakar, citing what the letter described as a conspiracy by "Islamic fundamentalist forces," according to LiveLaw.

What Happens Next

Under Indian law, a death sentence from a Sessions Court cannot be executed without confirmation from the High Court. All 13 sentences will now go before the Allahabad High Court for review. Research by the National Law University Delhi's Project 39A found that Indian trial courts sentenced over 1,300 people to death between 2014 and 2024, but High Courts upheld only 106 — and the Supreme Court did not confirm a single death sentence between 2023 and 2025.

The confirmation hearings, combined with potential appeals, mean the legal process for these 13 convicts is far from over. But the pace of Diwakar's sentencing has already reignited a broader debate: whether aggressive use of capital punishment at the trial court level delivers justice or creates a pattern that higher courts routinely reverse.
